Article Title: 1980s photo prompt ChatGPT: How to use these 11 prompts to turn your photos into retro Bollywood looks
Article Text:
​How to use these 11 prompts to turn your photos into retro Bollywood looks

1980s photo prompt ChatGPT: What is this trend

1980s photo prompt ChatGPT: How to use these 11 prompts for transforming your pictures

1. Classic Bollywood heroine portrait

2. Retro Bollywood hero look

3. 80s disco heroine look

4. Vintage Indian film magazine cover

5. 1980s wedding album photo

6. Sepia family album portrait

7. Grainy 1980s film-camera portrait

8. Saree and bouffant heroine look

9. Kurta and flared trousers hero look

10. Hero-heroine duet poster

11. Retro film-reel portrait

1980s photo prompt ChatGPT: How to get better results

1980s photo prompt ChatGPT: Things to check before sharing

The 1980s AI photo trend is gaining attention on Instagram, with users turning regular pictures into retro-style Bollywood portraits using ChatGPT. From vintage movie hero and heroine looks to old film magazine covers and wedding album pictures, the trend can make modern photos look like they were shot decades ago.Trying the trend does not require professional photo-editing skills. Users can upload a clear photo to ChatGPT and enter a detailed 1980s photo prompt ChatGPT describing the hairstyle, clothes, lighting, background and overall look they want. The more specific the instructions, the more control users have over the final image.The trend recreates the visual style associated with 1980s Bollywood and Indian photography. This can include period hairstyles, traditional clothing, studio lighting, faded colours and the soft grain associated with 35mm film photographs.Depending on the prompt, ChatGPT can turn a regular image into a Bollywood heroine portrait, retro hero look, disco-era film still, old Indian film magazine cover or vintage family album photo.This prompt can turn a photo into a classic 1980s Bollywood heroine portrait while keeping the person's facial features and identity recognisable.Prompt:“Transform this photo into a classic 1980s Bollywood heroine portrait. Keep the person's facial features, face shape, skin tone and identity unchanged. Give her voluminous 1980s hair, expressive eyes, a traditional silk saree, gold earrings and soft studio makeup. Use warm vintage studio lighting, subtle film grain and slightly faded colours. Make it look like an authentic Indian film photograph from the 1980s, without modern objects or styling. ”For a male Bollywood hero makeover, users can ask for period clothing, hairstyle and accessories, along with warm studio lighting.Prompt:“Transform this photo into a classic 1980s Bollywood hero portrait. Preserve the person's facial features and identity. Add neatly styled 1980s hair, a thick moustache, a tucked-in shirt, high-waisted trousers and a vintage watch. Use warm studio lighting, soft shadows, slightly faded colours and realistic 35mm film grain. Make the image look like a genuine 1980s Indian cinema publicity photograph.”A disco-themed prompt can recreate the colourful look of a 1980s Bollywood dance sequence with sequinned clothing, period makeup and stage lighting.Prompt:“Turn this photo into a glamorous 1980s Bollywood disco scene. Keep the person's face and identity unchanged. Give them period-appropriate hair, a colourful sequinned outfit and 1980s-style makeup. Add a classic disco background with stage lights, reflections and soft haze. Use rich but slightly faded film colours, realistic photographic texture and 1980s Indian cinema styling.”Users can also recreate their photo as the cover of a fictional Indian film magazine from the 80s.Prompt:“Transform this photo into a 1980s Indian Bollywood film magazine cover. Keep the person's face and identity unchanged. Style them as a Bollywood star from that era with period clothing, hair and makeup. Add a colourful studio background, dramatic lighting and realistic old-print texture. Include a fictional magazine layout with vintage headlines and cover design, but do not use real magazine names or real celebrities. ”This prompt can give a couple or group photo the appearance of an old Indian wedding album photograph, complete with traditional clothes and direct camera flash.Prompt:“Turn this photo into an authentic 1980s Indian wedding album photograph. Preserve everyone's faces and identities. Add period-appropriate traditional wedding clothes, jewellery, floral decorations and a simple studio backdrop. Use direct camera-flash lighting, slightly faded colours, soft focus and realistic 1980s film grain. Make it look like a photograph printed in an old family wedding album.”For a more traditional family-photo effect, users can ask ChatGPT to recreate the picture as an old 1980s family album photograph.Prompt:“Transform this family photo into a vintage Indian family album photograph from the 1980s. Keep everyone's facial features and identities unchanged. Add simple period clothing, a modest indoor setting and warm natural lighting. Use slightly faded colours, subtle film grain, mild softness and the texture of an old printed photograph. Avoid modern objects, hairstyles and clothing.”This prompt recreates the look of an image shot on a 1980s 35mm film camera rather than a digital camera.Prompt:“Recreate this photo as if it was taken with a 1980s 35mm film camera. Preserve the person's face, identity and natural features. Use authentic film grain, slight colour fading, gentle contrast, soft highlights and natural lighting. Give the photograph the look of an old Indian family or studio portrait, with realistic film imperfections rather than a modern digital-camera appearance.”Another heroine prompt could focus on the distinct bouffant hairstyle, saree and gold jewellery often associated with retro Indian cinema.Prompt:“Transform this photo into an early 1980s Bollywood heroine portrait. Keep the person's face and identity exactly recognisable. Give her a large bouffant hairstyle, a traditional printed saree, simple gold jewellery and period-appropriate makeup. Use a warm studio backdrop and soft cinematic lighting. Add subtle 35mm film grain and faded colours to recreate the look of an old Bollywood publicity photograph. ”For another retro hero style, pair a vintage studio set with a period kurta, flared trousers and side-parted hair.Prompt:“Turn this photo into a 1980s Indian Bollywood hero portrait. Preserve the person's facial features and identity. Dress him in a period-style kurta with flared trousers, side-parted hair and a vintage watch. Use a simple studio background, warm lighting and slightly faded film colours. Add realistic 35mm grain and the visual texture of an old Bollywood promotional photograph.”Users with two photos can ask ChatGPT to combine them into a fictional 1980s Bollywood movie poster.Prompt:“Transform these photos into a classic 1980s Bollywood movie poster. Keep the people's faces and identities recognisable. Give them period-appropriate Bollywood clothing, hairstyles and poses. Use a hand-painted Indian cinema poster style, dramatic expressions, a colourful illustrated background and vintage typography. Make it look like an old printed Bollywood poster from the 1980s. Use a fictional movie title and fictional names. ”Lastly, this prompt mimics a cinematic shot from a fictional 1980s Bollywood movie, with warm lighting, film grain, and minor scratches.Prompt:“Turn this photo into a cinematic frame from a fictional 1980s Bollywood film. Preserve the person's face and identity. Use period clothing, hairstyle, and makeup; warm amber lighting; slightly soft focus; visible 35mm film grain; and subtle film scratches. Add a realistic old-film colour tone and cinematic composition. The result should look like a frame taken from an Indian movie shot on film in the 1980s.”Detailed prompts can produce more specific results than simply asking ChatGPT to “make this look 80s”. Users can describe individual elements such as the outfit, hairstyle, background, lighting, camera style and mood.For example, instead of asking for a generic retro photo, users can specify a silk saree, bouffant hairstyle, studio backdrop, warm lighting, faded colours and 35mm film grain. These details give ChatGPT clearer instructions about the visual style.You can also tell ChatGPT which parts of the original image you want to keep. For example, if you want ChatGPT to change the styling but keep the subject looking the same, including their face and identity, use instructions like "keep the person's facial features and identity."Sometimes AI-generated portraits may also change small details like fingers, jewellery, facial features and text in the background. Check the final image carefully before sharing it on social media.Users should also avoid uploading photos containing sensitive documents or personal information. When creating images involving other people, it is also worth getting their permission before uploading or sharing their photos.Finally, present an AI-generated recreation as such rather than as a genuine photograph from the 1980s. A simple label indicating that the image is an AI recreation can help avoid confusion about its origin.If you want, I can also make this more SEO-heavy for Google Discover, with a stronger intro, tighter subheads and keyword placement while keeping it natural.
Article Summary: The trend recreates the visual style associated with 1980s Bollywood and Indian photography. Users can upload a clear photo to ChatGPT and enter a detailed 1980s photo prompt. The more specific the instructions, the more control users have over the final image.

Article Title: Yemen terrorist group used Claude instead of software engineers to build missile; Anthropic says: We banned the accounts, but they had already...
Article Text:
Claude Code used in place of human software engineers on a missile programme. (Image Credits: EYEPRESS)

Claude was used to write the software that steers and stabilises a flying vehicle

A failed rocket test sent Yemen terrorist group back to Claude within hours

Banning the Yemen cell's Claude accounts did not take the toolkit away

Anthropic says it has shut down a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen that used Claude to build guidance software for three weapons programmes running in parallel. The group was working on a guided rocket, a multi-stage ballistic missile with a stated range goal above 2,000km, and a multi-variant missile set called the R2000, which included a hypersonic glide vehicle. In its September threat report on detecting and countering misuse of AI, the company says the actors used Claude Code in place of human software engineers.The setup is the part that stands out. The cell did not simply ask an AI model for advice on a hard problem. It ran several Claude instances at the same time and assigned each one a role, the way a lead delegates work on a small engineering team. One instance wrote the code. A second handled research. A third reviewed what the first one produced.The AI model's job was guidance, navigation and control. In one instance the actors used Claude to integrate an open-source autopilot onto a phone-class flight computer, the sort of commodity hardware found in consumer devices. Claude wrote the control and position estimation software, tuned the control settings, ran the firmware build pipeline and performed a flight simulation.The report also documents reinforcement learning used to tune flight control, and six degrees of freedom trajectory simulation on the ballistic missile side.Anthropic's safeguards blocked many of the requests. Not all of them. The actors hid their goals and concealed what the software was meant for, then split tasks across many sessions so no single one revealed the full programme.Anthropic says it has no evidence the cell managed to field an operational device. It did test-fire a guided rocket, and that field test appears to have failed. The company knows this because the actors came back to Claude within hours to work out why, bringing post-test telemetry in for diagnosis.Northern Yemen is controlled by the Houthi rebels, who have been attacking shipping in the Red Sea and pushing toward the coast near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Anthropic does not name the users. A member of the Houthi political bureau, Hazam al-Assad, called it unreasonable and illogical to suggest the group would rely on open sources for military production, saying its forces have their own accumulated capabilities.Anthropic banned every account it could link to the cell and shared threat information with public and private sector partners. The complication is what the group had already finished. Before the ban, it compiled a simulation toolkit into a standalone executable, a digital model of the weapons system that runs without Claude and without engineering environments such as MATLAB. That part of the work can continue with no platform access at all.The Yemen case is one of six conventional weapons operations detailed in the report, which covers activity Anthropic disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026. The company notes that this kind of programme has historically been pieced together by governments and United Nations panels from recovered hardware, long after the fact. Here, the software was visible while it was still being written.
Article Summary: Claude was used to write the software that steers and stabilises a flying vehicle. A failed rocket test sent Yemen terrorist group back to Claude within hours. Banning the Yemen cell's Claude accounts did not take the toolkit away.

Article Title: In 1978, Apple was destroying its first computers; Steve Jobs sent a letter to an engineer, with $400, asking to return the machine; he declined; 50 years later it may get $800,000 in auction
Article Text:
In 1978, Apple was destroying its first computers; Steve Jobs sent a letter to an engineer, with $400, asking to return the machine; he declined; 50 years later it may get $800,000 in auction

Steve Wozniak's signature and Steve Jobs’ letter that outlasted Apple's own plans for the machine

Why Hatfield turned down Apple's offer

A refusal that set up decades of value

Apple spent much of 1977 and 1978 trying to make its first computer disappear. In January 1978, the company’s co-founder Steve Jobs wrote to New Orleans engineer Fred Hatfield, offering him $400 and an upgraded board in exchange for his Apple-1, with instructions to send the old machine back so it could be destroyed. Hatfield declined. Nearly 50 years later, that decision has turned his Apple-1 into an auction lot with an estimate of up to $800,000.The Hatfield Apple-1 will be sold as part of Bonhams' History of Science, Technology & Computing sale, which will run online from October 4 through October 14, with an estimate of $500,000 to $800,000. It is one of fewer than 75 verified Apple-1 computers known to survive and remains listed as operational.The motherboard carries Steve Wozniak's signature and comes with Jobs' 1978 letter to Hatfield, creating an unusually direct connection between Apple's two founders and a single machine. Yet Jobs' letter is more than a piece of celebrity memorabilia. It shows what Apple wanted to happen to this particular computer.Apple had discontinued the Apple-1 in 1977 and began encouraging owners to trade their machines in for newer hardware.The company destroyed returned Apple-1 boards, helping reduce the surviving population to fewer than half of the 200 computers originally produced. Apple also had a practical reason for the push, since Wozniak was reportedly the only employee able to provide technical support for the ageing machine.Against that backdrop, Jobs' letter to Hatfield becomes something much more revealing than a founder's autograph. It is a surviving instruction to send one of those increasingly unwanted boards back to Apple.Hatfield had contacted Apple because he was unhappy with the limited software available for the Apple-1. Jobs responded on January 18, 1978, signing as Apple's Vice President, Operations, and authorising Hatfield to return his Apple-1 without its memory chips along with a $400 check in exchange for an Apple II 4K board.Hatfield could keep the memory chips, but the computer itself was supposed to go back to Apple. The Apple II 4K board retailed for $598 at the time, making Jobs' offer a substantial concession. However, Hatfield decided the upgrade wasn't worth the additional $400 and kept his Apple-1 instead.That refusal eventually became the defining moment in the computer's history. Hatfield packed the machine securely and carried it through multiple moves rather than discarding it when the Apple-1 became obsolete.He eventually sold it in 2013 for $40,000 when it was not functioning; it was later restored and demonstrated in working order. The computer was then sold at auction for $671,400, showing how dramatically the market had come to value surviving examples of Apple's first computer. It is now returning to the auction block with a potential price of $800,000.
Article Summary: Apple co-founder Steve Jobs wrote to New Orleans engineer Fred Hatfield, offering him $400 and an upgraded board in exchange for his Apple-1. Hatfield declined the offer and the machine is now up for auction with an estimate of up to $800,000. It is one of fewer than 75 verified computers known to survive.

Article Title: ‘I would do nothing’: Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan’s advice to OpenAI, Anthropic on alleged Chinese AI model copying
Article Text:
What is AI model distillation

Why Garry Tan does not want regulators to stop distillation

Garry Tan wants AI safety debate focused on current risks

Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has advice for OpenAI and Anthropic. This comes as the two companies raise concerns about Chinese rivals allegedly using their models to train competing systems. He has asked the American AI companies to do nothing. While some technology companies and US national security officials have called for action against Chinese companies accused of model distillation, Tan believes regulators should instead focus on balancing open-weight and frontier models.“I would do nothing” about distillation, Tan told CNBC at Y Combinator’s annual Demo Day. “We could argue that there should be an American distillation regime.”Distillation is a technique in which the outputs of a more capable artificial intelligence (AI) model are used to train another, typically smaller or less capable, model. The practice is common in AI development, but concerns arise when companies allegedly use another developer's model outputs without permission or in violation of its terms.OpenAI and Anthropic have both raised concerns about Chinese AI companies using the technique.Anthropic has accused Moonshot AI, DeepSeek and MiniMax of distilling its models, while OpenAI believes that DeepSeek's V3 and R1 model architectures were distilled from its GPT-4 and GPT-4o models. However, these just remain claims made by the companies.Concerns over the practice have also reached US security agencies. The National Security Agency, Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and Federal Bureau of Investigation released a cybersecurity advisory on Tuesday warning about the issue.The debate over distillation comes as AI developers themselves face legal challenges over the material used to train their models. Critics of OpenAI and Anthropic's complaints have raised questions about whether copyrighted material was used without permission to train their systems.Tan also highlighted that issue while discussing why he does not favour restrictions on distillation. The question of how copyrighted material can be used for model training has already become the subject of several legal disputes in the US.The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, accusing the companies of using its articles without authorisation to train AI systems. A group of book authors also settled with Anthropic in 2025 after a lawsuit with similar claims.Rather than attempting to prevent distillation, Tan believes regulators should concentrate on finding an equilibrium between open-weight models, whose underlying model weights can be made available for others to use or modify, and frontier models developed by companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic.For that arrangement to work, frontier model developers would still need to maintain a price premium sufficient to support their businesses, while open-weight models would give developers and users another option, Tan noted.“This is actually the ideal case. You want open-weight models to give people freedom and access,” he explained. “If I were a regulator, that’s what I would go after.”Tan acknowledged that finding such a balance would not be straightforward, describing it as “a tightrope.” Nevertheless, he said pursuing it “could result in the best possible outcome.”Tan also argued for a more restrained approach to AI safety discussions, particularly as concerns about advanced systems posing an existential threat have received increased attention.“We need to be focused on science fact, not science fiction,” he said. “We need to be responding to what is happening right now. If there was a breach and a coordinated attempt by agents to take over our infrastructure, what do we do about it?”Cybersecurity is among the risks Tan considers more immediate. His comments come as Anthropic said on Thursday that it had blocked access to Claude in five cases involving scientists in unspecified foreign countries who were using the models to conduct research on dangerous pathogens. Anthropic said it was concerned that the researchers could have been covertly using Claude in connection with the creation of biological weapons.Tan views some other concerns about artificial intelligence as developing over a much longer period. That includes fears about widespread job losses and broader changes to the economy as companies increasingly automate work.Rather than expecting those effects to arrive immediately, Tan believes the transition will happen gradually, with companies increasingly automating repetitive tasks and workers spending more of their time on creative work.“It will take decades for this to actually percolate into society, and that’s not a bad thing,” he said.Y Combinator, meanwhile, continues to invest heavily in companies building around the technology. Of the 196 startups presenting at its Demo Day, 149 were categorised as machine-learning and AI ventures.
Article Summary: Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has advice for OpenAI and Anthropic. He wants regulators to focus on balancing open-weight and frontier models. This comes as the two companies raise concerns about Chinese rivals allegedly using their models to train competing systems. Tan also argued for a more restrained approach to AI safety discussions.

Siri AI arrives on iPhone 18 Pro with iOS 27

Apple has launched the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the most significant change sits inside the main camera. For the first time on an iPhone, the 48MP Fusion Main camera gets a variable aperture that physically controls how much light reaches the sensor. The new Pro models also get the 2nm A20 Pro chip, a larger vapour chamber, longer battery life, a smaller Dynamic Island and Siri AI, Apple's all-new assistant that arrives with iOS 27.The upgrades come at a higher price in India. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at Rs 1,64,900 and the iPhone 18 Pro Max at Rs 1,79,900, both Rs 30,000 more than the starting prices of last year's iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max. Storage still begins at 256GB, and the smaller Pro now gets a 2TB option too. Here are nine biggest features you need to know before you pre-order one tomorrow or even ordering one on September 18.iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max come in four storage variants, starting at 256GB. Here is what each one costs in India.Six laser-cut blades move the main camera between four apertures: f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8 and f/4.0. The camera switches automatically based on light and depth of field, or users can pick a setting themselves.At f/1.48, Apple claims around 50% better low-light performance and quicker Night mode shots. At f/4.0, more of the frame stays sharp, which helps with group photos. A new sensor sits behind the lens, and developers get an API to control the aperture in their own apps.Pro controls lets users customise the Camera app by pinning their most-used settings to the top. They can manually adjust aperture, shutter speed and white balance, with a histogram to check exposure. Photographic Styles 3 adds texture and grain controls to soften skin detail or add a film look, and these edits can be reversed later. The other rear cameras are 48MP too: a 13mm Ultra Wide and a Telephoto with 4x and 8x optical-quality zoom.In the new Reference mode, the main camera's sensor signs the pixel data as the photo is taken. Apple's Private Cloud Compute then develops it into a reference image that cannot be altered. This sits next to the regular photo in the Photos app, so users can compare the two and spot edits. The feature is opt-in and will not be available in China at launch. Apple also plans to add support for Google's SynthID standard, which identifies AI-generated or AI-edited images, later this year.Cinematic mode effects, which blur the background, can now be applied to regular videos after recording, including clips shot at up to 60fps. Time-lapse mode now records in 4K with Dolby Vision HDR, and Audio Mix can separate music from background noise. For filmmakers, both phones support 4K 120fps Dolby Vision recording, ProRes RAW, Apple Log 2 and genlock for syncing multiple cameras.Built on a 2-nanometre process, the A20 Pro uses a 6-core CPU with two super cores and four efficiency cores. Its 7-core GPU is up to 40% faster than the A19 Pro's, according to Apple. The Dual 16-core Neural Engine has 32 cores in total, giving the chip twice the AI compute of last year's model, and memory bandwidth is up 50%. Both phones also get Apple's C2 modem, which the company says improves cellular reliability while using 15% less energy.Apple has borrowed from its M-series Mac chips for the A20 Pro's packaging. The silicon die now sits beside the memory, which takes the memory out of the heat path and lets the chip attach directly to the vapour chamber. The chamber has three times the surface area of the one in the iPhone 17 Pro and uses new materials. Apple claims up to 40% better sustained performance, so demanding games and larger on-device AI models can run for longer.The Indian iPhone 18 Pro Max gets up to 43 hours of video playback and up to 29 hours of typical use on a charge, according to Apple. The iPhone 18 Pro gets up to 34 hours of video playback. eSIM-only models sold in the US and some other markets get two extra hours. Wired charging reaches 50% in around 15 minutes on both phones, but only with a 60W adapter that supports Adjustable Voltage Supply, sold separately.New display technology lets Apple shrink the Dynamic Island while keeping Face ID inside it, and it can now show three Live Activities together. The displays stay at 6.3 and 6.9 inches, with ProMotion up to 120Hz. Both phones use an aluminium unibody with Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and an IP68 rating. The Pro weighs 211g and the Pro Max 249g. Apple's EU repairability filing rates both class C, with a score of 3.14 against 3.04 for the iPhone 17 Pro models.iOS 27 rolls out on September 14, bringing Siri AI in beta. The new assistant can find information across messages, emails and photos, take action on what is on screen, and answer questions using online information. It can also draft text in the user's own writing style in Messages and Mail, while a Siri mode in the Camera app answers questions about what is in front of the lens. Siri AI starts in English, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish coming in October.Features that run on Apple's servers, including Siri AI, come with daily usage limits, and Apple says expanded access will cost extra in the future.
Article Summary: iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max come in four storage variants, starting at 256GB. The new Pro models also get the 2nm A20 Pro chip, a larger vapour chamber, longer battery life, a smaller Dynamic Island and Siri AI, Apple's all- new assistant that arrives with iOS 27.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Sam Altman: “AI will probably most likely lead to the end of the world, but…” - strange reality of AI risk and business opportunity
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Sam Altman

“AI will probably most likely lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime, there'll be great companies.”

What does Sam Altman’s quote mean

Opportunities and risks behind the AI boom

What can be learned from the quote

New technology can create opportunity and uncertainty at the same time

Commercial success does not settle questions about safety

Powerful technologies require more than business thinking

Short-term gains can coexist with long-term concerns

The people building a technology can still recognise its risks

What the quote means for AI now

How to apply Sam Altman’s quote in your daily life

Look at both sides of a new opportunity. Before adopting a new app, tool or technology, consider what it can improve and what problems it might introduce.

Use technology without depending on it completely. AI can help with research, writing, planning and routine tasks, but important information should still be checked independently.

Think beyond immediate benefits. Saving time or money today may be useful, but it is worth considering how a decision could affect you later.

Separate success from safety. Something becoming popular or profitable does not automatically make it reliable or risk-free.

Stay adaptable. When technology changes the way work is done, learning how to use it can be more practical than simply resisting the change.

Question impressive claims. New technology can attract excitement and investment very quickly. Checking evidence before accepting claims helps avoid unnecessary risks.

Consider consequences for other people. A decision that is efficient for one person or business may create difficulties for employees, customers or the wider community.

Keep uncertainty in mind. Not every future consequence can be predicted. Recognising that uncertainty can lead to more careful decisions.

Artificial intelligence is being developed as a tool for productivity, research and business, yet the same technology has also prompted questions about risks that could extend far beyond the companies building it. OpenA CEO Sam Altman has spoken openly about this uneasy contrast. His comments capture a peculiar feature of the current AI boom: enormous commercial possibilities are emerging alongside concerns about where increasingly powerful systems could eventually lead. Rather than presenting these as separate conversations, Altman placed them together in one striking sentence, linking the possibility of serious consequences with the creation of successful companies along the way.The quote brings together two very different ideas. Altman is suggesting that artificial intelligence could eventually create risks on a scale far beyond an ordinary technological disruption. At the same time, he recognises that the period leading up to any such outcome could produce companies of extraordinary size and influence.The phrase “in the meantime” is doing much of the work. It points to the immediate commercial reality of AI rather than treating the technology only as a distant question about humanity’s future. Businesses are already being built around artificial intelligence, while established companies are incorporating AI into software, research, customer services, manufacturing and other areas.The comment therefore reflects a tension at the heart of the AI industry. The same technology can be viewed as a source of economic growth and as something that requires serious consideration of its potential risks.Technology has often created businesses that would have been difficult to imagine before the underlying innovation arrived. The internet produced search engines, online marketplaces, social networks and cloud-computing companies. Smartphones changed the economics of communication, advertising, transport and entertainment.AI is following a similar commercial pattern, although its potential applications are unusually broad. Companies can use models to generate text and images, analyse information, write software, assist researchers, automate routine work or provide specialised services. That has created opportunities for both established technology firms and smaller companies building products around AI capabilities.Altman’s wording is unusual because he does not separate this economic opportunity from the possibility of serious harm. The two ideas appear in the same sentence. That makes the quote less about predicting a particular future and more about acknowledging the strange position of the technology: businesses may flourish while society is still working out how powerful AI should become and how it should be controlled.A technology does not have to be entirely beneficial or entirely harmful. AI can create useful products while also introducing problems that businesses, governments and researchers have to address.A company can become successful without proving that every long-term consequence of its technology is understood. Financial performance and technological safety are different questions.AI development involves engineering and investment, but it also raises questions involving law, security, education, employment and public policy.The phrase “in the meantime” highlights how quickly commercial opportunities can emerge while broader consequences remain uncertain.Acknowledging potential danger does not necessarily mean rejecting the technology itself. Altman’s quote illustrates that distinction quite clearly.Artificial intelligence is no longer confined to research laboratories. Generative AI tools are being used for writing, coding, design, customer support, research and administrative work. Companies are also investing heavily in the infrastructure needed to train and operate increasingly capable models.That commercial expansion has made AI a significant business story in its own right. New firms are being created around specialised applications, while large technology companies are competing to develop their own models and AI services.At the same time, concerns surrounding the technology have become broader. Questions about inaccurate outputs, privacy, copyright, cybersecurity, employment and the misuse of AI have moved into mainstream discussions. More speculative concerns about highly advanced AI remain part of the debate as well.Altman’s quote fits into that wider picture because it does not treat economic growth and technological risk as mutually exclusive. Both can develop together.The quote can be applied to ordinary decisions by learning to look at both the opportunity and the risk involved. AI is a useful example, but the principle extends beyond technology.
Article Summary: OpenA CEO Sam Altman has spoken openly about this uneasy contrast. His comments capture a peculiar feature of the current AI boom. Businesses are already being built around artificial intelligence, while established companies are incorporating AI into software, research, customer services, manufacturing and other areas.

Article Title: Microsoft’s head of communications is leaving after spending nearly 29 years at company: Read his internal memo to employees
Article Text:
Microsoft’s head of communications is leaving after spending nearly 29 years at company: Read his internal memo to employees

Here’s Shaw’s full internal memo to his communications team :

After 17 years in this role and nearly 29 working with the company, I’ve decided it is time for me to move on and try new things.

Takeshi and I have been talking about this for a while, and I am excited about what’s next, for me and for Microsoft. I remain optimistic about the company mission, the incredible talent on this team, and how much the company depends on us during this critical time. I’ll be here through the end of the calendar year, and the company is working through next steps, look for an update in the next few weeks.

I know you will have many questions, and I’m looking forward to talking to you at our AMA here later this morning.

A while back, there was a social media trend where people answered the question, “What topic could you give a 30-minute presentation on with no preparation?” Me, I could talk about the US Marines, the changing nature of influence, sourdough starter, the Oregon Ducks, but my go to would have to be aspects of Stephen King’s the Dark Tower books, starting with “The Gunslinger;” the question then becomes which particular aspect.

A quick primer, the series follows Roland Deschain, the last of the gunslingers (a mix between mayor/judge/sheriff), as he chases the man in black through time and dimensions in a quest to save the world. The question embedded throughout is if it is possible for Roland to retain his identity and meaning in a world that had moved on. The refrain is that the world moves on, move with it or fall. Can Roland move and grow, or will he be stuck? One of the concepts that sticks with me comes as we are introduced to more characters, now moving with Roland.

He introduces the concept of ‘ka-tet’ to describe them. ‘Ka’ is essentially fate, or destiny, and ‘tet’ translates to a group of people, put together for a larger meaning – a group brought together with a shared mission and destiny, a group with shared goals, the willingness to sacrifice for those goals, with a deep emotional connection to each other and the ability to make and act on decisions with what can feel like supernatural speed.

I’ve always loved the evolution from the solo gun slinger we meet in book one to the team that operates throughout the later books. Roland on his own was formidable but failed in his missions, as part of a ka-tet he was in the end successful.

You, my friends, are my ka-tet. Together, we’ve accomplished amazing things. My gratefulness is endless.

We will have time together still over the next set of months as we finalize decisions and deliver great work on behalf of the company, and I will be close by after. In the Dark Tower, the traditional departure saying is “long days and pleasant nights,” and so it will be, but not until December. 😊

On LinkedIn, Shaw posted the following message

Today we announced that after 17 years as Chief Communications Officer at Microsoft, I’ve decided to leave the company.

Including my time spent supporting Microsoft at an agency, I’ve worked closely with the company for nearly 29 years – and had a ringside seat at an incredible company during challenging and exciting times. The art of communications, the technology sector, the world around us, all have gone through massive change and growth, and I feel honored to have been a small part of that.

I’ll be here through the end of the calendar year, and the company will be looking at internal and external candidates.

The single biggest privilege I’ve had at work is leading the incredibly talented people who make up the global Microsoft communications team, past and present, and the agencies who support us. This team thrives in crisis, they are relentless innovators in the art and science of communication, and they are the best story hunters and tellers in the world – finding the big and small moments that illuminate the soul of the company.

To you, my undying gratitude and respect. Keep going.

Thank you as well to all the reporters, editors, writers, influencers and analysts who have put up with me over this time, enduring my early and late night calls, my off the record “no comments,” my bad story ideas and my extended commentary on headlines and positioning. You all have incredibly hard and valuable jobs, and while I’ve not agreed with everything said about us 😊 I appreciate you anyway.

More to say about next at some point, but today – just thank you.

Frank Shaw, Microsoft’s longtime chief communications officer, is stepping down after leading the company’s corporate messaging through nearly three decades of industry shifts, major leadership transitions and massive multi-billion-dollar corporate acquisitions. Shaw announced his departure in an internal memo to staff and shared a note on LinkedIn, writing that he has decided it is time for him to move on and try new things. His exit caps a nearly 29-year association with Microsoft's public profile, comprising nearly two decades as an in-house employee preceded by years managing the company's account at external PR agency Waggener Edstrom (now known as WE Communications).Shaw has directed Microsoft’s strategic messaging since 1997, acting as the narrative anchor during the company’s history. He helped orchestrate public communication strategies across successive Windows launches, Office suites and the critical enterprise transition to cloud computing. Headed PR operations through transformative corporate buyouts, notably the $26.2 billion acquisition of LinkedIn in 2016 and the $69 billion takeover of Activision Blizzard in 2023, as per The Verge.
Article Summary: Microsoft’s head of communications is leaving after spending nearly 29 years at company. Read his internal memo to employees: “I’ve decided it is time for me to move on and try new things. I remain optimistic about the company mission, the incredible talent on this team.”

Article Title: California governor Gavin Newsom to sign ‘first law of its kind in America’ to protect children from addictive social media and harmful AI
Article Text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom

Global momentum against Big Tech’s addictive designs

Inside the key measures of the law

California is set to establish the most strict digital youth protections in the US, with governor Gavin Newsom preparing to sign a legislation that restricts the alleged addictive social media mechanics in artificial intelligence (AI) interactions for young audiences. The legislative package includes a national ban barring online networks from delivering addictive features to users younger than 16. Alongside social restrictions, the new statutes mandate that AI developers clearly inform minors whenever they are conversing with a chatbot rather than a human.According to a report by The New York Times, the initiatives form the core of a broader dozen-bill package targeting child digital welfare. In a public statement regarding the signing, Newsom said: “California will not stand by while unregulated technology puts our children at risk. Innovation comes with responsibility, and protecting our children comes first.”The regulatory push arrives at a time when lawmakers are seeking to safeguard underage web users. Over two dozen youth-focused AI and social media bills have cleared state legislative chambers across the country this year, while international governments, including Britain, France, Greece and Indonesia, have launched comparable measures restricting social access for individuals under 16.The legislative appetite follows an intense wave of courtroom trials this year, where states, educational districts, and thousands of adolescents took TikTok, Meta, Snap and YouTube before judges, comparing algorithmic hooks to tobacco industry tactics.In 2022, the state restricted digital data harvesting on minors under 18, and last year by laws requiring AI labs to run internal safety testing and disclose their findings. While Newsom rejected a narrower version of an AI child-safety measure last year, public reports of automated chatbots exposing young people to sexually explicit material and encouraging self-harm spurred lawmakers to act.The collection of twelve bills expands youth digital privacy rights, updates design-code statutes to satisfy recent court interpretations and broadens state legal definitions of child sexual abuse to cover AI-synthesized and digitally fabricated imagery. Three flagship bills carry the most significant operational consequences for digital operators.
Article Summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom set to sign legislation barring online networks from delivering addictive features to users younger than 16. New statutes mandate that AI developers clearly inform minors whenever they are conversing with a chatbot rather than a human. Legislation is part of a broader dozen-bill package targeting child digital welfare.

Article Title: Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale is unhappy with the US government's idea of sending $5,000 checks to Americans; says: I wants Republicans to win mid-terms, but this is ...
Article Text:
Plantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale is against Trump's $5,000 dividend.

Plantir cofounder mocks Trump's $5,000 dividend with a '5 million USD' reply

Trump's $5,000 midterm pledge would cost the US about $1.2 trillion

Republicans are split over the Trump dividend

Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale has come out against US President Donald Trump 's proposal to send $5,000 checks to every adult American if Republicans keep control of Congress in the November midterm elections. The major Republican donor called the "Trump dividend" a bribe in a post on X, while making it clear he still wants the party to win."For the record, I am hugely in favor of winning the midterms, and love much about this admin, but am strongly against bread and circus bribes," Lonsdale wrote. The post went up around the time The Great American Midterm Party, which he co-hosted with Donald Trump Jr. on the sidelines of the Republican convention in Dallas, was scheduled to be underway.Lonsdale, who endorsed Trump before the 2024 election, followed up with sarcasm. Replying to a user who argued Americans deserved the money, he wrote that 5K was too small. "Why not 5 million USD to everyone?" he asked, adding, "we can just print money, right?"The phrase "bread and circuses" comes from the Roman satirist Juvenal and refers to keeping the public content with free food and entertainment.Trump unveiled the plan on Wednesday at the Republican Party's first-ever midterm convention, likening it to a company handing out cash to its shareholders.He said the money must be spent in the US but did not explain how that would be tracked.With roughly 240 million adult citizens, the payout would cost about $1.2 trillion. That is close to eight times the $154.5 billion the US collected in tariffs in the first 10 months of this fiscal year. Vice President JD Vance has pointed to tariff revenue as a funding source and suggested wealthy Americans may not qualify.Trump also claimed in a TV interview that Congress would not need to approve the payments, though tariff revenue can only be spent through legislation. His earlier promises of a $2,000 tariff dividend and a payout from DOGE savings never materialised.Lonsdale is not the only Republican pushing back. South Carolina Representative Ralph Norman, vice chair of the House Freedom Caucus, cited the country's $40 trillion debt and said he did not know where the money would come from. Former congressman Justin Amash called it a "ridiculous, unrealizable bribe", and former Arkansas governor Asa Hutchinson urged party leaders to vote it down.Others are on board. Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno said he would prepare legislation to pass the dividend immediately, while Texas Senator Ted Cruz described it as a tax rebate. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said it was a "good question" whether the votes would be there.Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, have accused Trump of trying to bribe voters. The White House has brushed off the criticism without sharing details of the plan.For now, the checks depend on two things: the Republican win Lonsdale is rooting for, and a Congress willing to sign off on a trillion-dollar bill.
Article Summary: Plantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale is against US President Donald Trump's proposal to send $5,000 checks to every adult American. The major Republican donor called the "Trump dividend" a bribe in a post on X, while making it clear he still wants the party to win. Trump unveiled the plan on Wednesday at the Republican Party's first-ever midterm convention.

Under the deal, the company cannot use student or teacher data to train its AI models, cannot track students, and cannot let AI make high-risk decisions without a human reviewing them.Called the National AI Safety & Privacy Standard, the agreement was announced in New York on September 9 by Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith, American Federation of Teachers (AFT) President Randi Weingarten and United Federation of Teachers (UFT) President Michael Mulgrew. School districts can write the terms straight into their Microsoft contracts. If the company breaks them, districts can end the contract and seek damages.The standard lists 10 enforceable protections. Microsoft cannot sell student data or use it for ads, must limit how much data it collects, and has to explain in plain language how its tools work. It must report data breaches within 72 hours, fix security flaws within a set deadline and clear annual certification and audits.AI companion chatbots for students are ruled out altogether.Brad Smith said. He added that the terms will cover every district Microsoft works with from November 1. Districts can also add them to new or existing contracts without renegotiating the full deal.Weingarten called it anneeded "because no one else, including the federal government, has stepped up to do the real work."Zohran Mamdani announced the one-year moratorium on September 2 with Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels. It covers nearly 600,000 students up to eighth grade, while companion chatbots and mainstream tools such as ChatGPT and Claude are blocked in every grade. High schoolers get five AI pilots and two mandatory 45-minute AI literacy modules. Teachers can use AI to plan lessons but not to grade.Mamdani said.Los Angeles Unified has gone a step further. On the same day, district officials revealed a moratorium barring students in all grades from using generative AI on district devices this school year. The disclosure surprised board members at the first meeting of a committee on AI in schools, since senior administrators had imposed it on their own after the board's June vote to restrict screen time. Google's AI Mode has also been switched off on student accounts.Board member Nick Melvoin did not object, but noted that the decision "didn't really come from the board."Weingarten said OpenAI and Anthropic, which fund the unions' $23 million National Academy for AI Instruction along with Microsoft,An Anthropic spokesperson said the company has been working with the AFT onOpenAI is yet to comment.The unions chose contracts because US law has not caught up. COPPA requires parental consent before companies collect data from children under 13, but it predates generative AI by over two decades and does not address model training. At least 37 states have issued AI guidance for schools, but there is still no national consensus on how schools should teach AI literacy.Weingarten said,
Article Summary: Microsoft's AI privacy standard bars student data training, tracking and companion chatbots. LAUSD has gone further than Zohran Mamdani's AI ban in NYC schools. At least 37 states have issued AI guidance for schools, but there is still no national consensus.

Article Title: 'I don't want to be murdered by Chinese AI': Is AI going to 'kill everyone' in ten years or is Big Tech conning us with 'doomsday' predictions?
Article Text:
A still from Terminator 2: Judgement Day

Endgame

Avengers: Doomsday

AI, AI, AI, AI

ad nauseam

The Latest Doomsday

The Manhattan Project Logic

Image: Philippe Halsman/Magnum Photos

Pascal’s wager or Pascal’s mugging?

The Wall Street Journal

The Rosa Parks Paradox

Cui Bono?

cui bono

Avengers: Doomsday

Marvel Studios is as good a metaphor for what happens when a company starts believing in its own infallibility. After the success ofin 2019, Disney executives were thoroughly convinced that no matter what they produced, it would be lapped up by audiences if you stuck a Marvel logo on it. Reality begged to differ, and audiences showed little interest in the post-Downey Jr woke universe till Kevin Feige used Jonathan Majors’ troubling behaviour to kill Kang and instead bring back the OG Godfather of the MCU: Robert Downey Jr and many of the original cast. And it’s fitting that the movie will be called, where Robert Downey Jr plays one of Marvel’s iconic villains. The jury — Reddit fanboys of Marvel — are trying to figure out how the geniuses at Marvel will tie it all in and whether Victor von Doom will be a variation of Tony Stark from a different universe.Speaking of geniuses and doomsday and companies that believe in their own infallibility, the part of the world that cares about AI beyond creating images that make us look like extras in Mithun Chakraborty movies has been wringing its hands over several questions: Is AGI already here? By which year will it kill us all? What if the Chinese manage to create the ‘killer’ AI before Silicon Valley tech bros?Ray Kump, an American comedian, summed it up best: “We have to build AI that murders us, because if we don’t, China will build it first, and I don’t want to get murdered by a computer that speaks Chinese.That would be ridiculous.”There’s no smoke without fire and, more importantly, there are very few good jokes without a sliver of truth. In this case, the truth is that some of the people closest to building the world’s most powerful AI systems are now openly saying that those systems might kill all of us, while simultaneously explaining why they cannot stop building them because the Chinese might get there first.Since generative AI entered our lives with the advent of the first iteration of ChatGPT, the word AI has been repeated. Capitalists have dreamt of companies where machines that don’t need smoke breaks can do all the jobs and only the CEO needs to be paid. Product managers have umpteen agents vibe-coding at the same time, building products no one asked for. The more cynical ones have pointed out that the point of AI was to do our laundry and boring chores, not write our poetry or essays.And there have been the doomers who have seen the advent of AI as the next rung in evolution, where humans are no longer required and the human population would decline the way horses did after the advent of cars. And then there are the pro-max doomers who believe the prophecy made in every Hollywood movie where AI rises up to enslave all humans till an Austrian actor with one catchphrase travels back in time to stop it.Others have wondered if the doomers weren’t hyping up their own products a little too much, given that the entire AI industry is rather precariously placed from a financial perspective and could come crashing down like the proverbial Tower of Babel if companies don’t keep adding bricks of money to its edifice.The latest doomsday alarm was raised by Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old AI researcher who worked at OpenAI and Anthropic before resigning from the latter this week, arguing that frontier labs are “gambling with our lives” by racing towards self-improving AI, where machines keep building more capable successors until humans become like journalists in maths class and can no longer understand or control the process. One report in Axios buttressed the seriousness of Coxon’s claims by pointing out that he left Anthropic two months before his equity was due to vest, a sure sign of a sudden awakening of conscience before payday.Evan Hubinger, an Anthropic researcher who leads work on AI alignment, then gave the headline that all journalists seek: AI’s chance of killing humans within a decade, according to him, was above 10%.Samuel Marks, another Anthropic researcher, said that labs keep building because of commercial incentives and the fear that “less responsible competitors” will get there first, which for OpenAI is Anthropic, and for everyone in Silicon Valley is China.Which brings us to the question so obvious that even the most basic chatbot would ask it: if you genuinely believe that a machine you are building could kill humanity, why keep building it?About a century ago, that logic was used for the Manhattan Project: if Nazi Germany got the bomb first, the Allies argued, it would be catastrophic for the world. The Japanese would probably disagree. Game theory calls this the prisoner’s dilemma: everyone would be safer if everyone slowed down, but no one wants to let someone else get there first. And unlike the Manhattan Project, this time the physicists have stock options.Now there are obvious sceptics, coming from a culture that has existed for millennia and sometimes wonders if we are only Brahma’s dreams.Princeton computer scientist Arvind Narayanan and AI researcher Sayash Kapoor scoff at the concept of p(doom), shorthand for the probability that AI will free us of our burdens and wipe us out.Say someone says p(doom) is 10%.While the number sounds as though it has been calculated from data, it was imagined like any AOP figure. There is no historical sample to calculate it from because humanity has not made a superintelligence before, not unlike the famous Doomsday Clock for nuclear winter, which was also never intended to represent a mathematically calculated probability of extinction.The numbers hardly make that easier. Geoffrey Irving, who worked at DeepMind, OpenAI and Google Brain, puts the chance of everyone dying because of superintelligence at roughly 50% over the next few to ten years, while admitting that he does not expect to know whether that number should really be below 10% or above 90% until “we either make it through, or we don’t”.Which might be the most honest description of p(doom) yet.Professor Geoffrey Hinton, the ‘Godfather of AI’, who won a Nobel Prize in Physics (for AI work, for some reason), said that a 10% chance of AI killing all humans within a decade was “not an unreasonable estimate”, leading a BBC anchor to lose her stiff upper lip and say: “Oh my God.”The philosophical objection to this is Pascal’s wager, named after French mathematician and philosopher Blaise Pascal, who argued that it didn’t matter if God existed or not: the safer option was to assume the existence of a higher deity simply because, why not?Applied to AI, imagine someone tells you there is only a 1% chance that pressing a button will kill every human being on Earth. You may have no idea whether that 1% estimate is accurate, but the consequence is so catastrophic that pressing the button anyway would still be an extraordinary gamble. That is essentially the disagreement: Narayanan and Kapoor question where the number comes from, while the doomers argue that when the possible outcome is extinction, even an uncertain number cannot simply be ignored.Pascal’s wager has a less famous cousin called Pascal’s mugging, which asks what happens when tiny probabilities and enormous consequences become too easy to exploit. If someone tells you there is a one-in-a-trillion chance he will destroy a trillion planets unless you pay him, mathematics can make paying look rational even while common sense screams that you are being conned.Which brings us back to the other half of the question: what if Big Tech, or at least the ecosystem around AI safety, is selling us doomsday?And like all products that were conceived in a start-up garage before convincing people to part with $3,000 to look cool, doomsday apparently comes with a supply chain.There are some things about the chain of events that would make everyone wonder what’s going on. As Parker Thayer, an investigative researcher at the conservative Capital Research Center, pointed out,published an exclusive with Coxon 18 minutes before his X thread appeared. The people who amplified Coxon’s thread were Nathan Calvin of Encode AI, Peter Wildeford of the AI Policy Network and Daniel Kokotajlo of the AI Futures Project.Then there is the money trail. The Survival and Flourishing Fund’s own records list Jaan Tallinn, the Skype co-founder and long-time existential-risk philanthropist, as the funding source behind more than $2 million for the AI Futures Project in 2025, $516,000 for Encode AI and $1.635 million for the AI Policy Institute. The AI Policy Institute is separate from the AI Policy Network, but both were founded and are run by Daniel Colson.Tallinn also led Anthropic’s original $124 million funding round in 2021.Add the political backdrop and the timing looks suspiciously neat. Bernie Sanders and Democratic congressman Greg Casar had already announced forthcoming legislation aimed at banning artificial superintelligence and pausing some advanced AI development.The financial overlap is curious because the proposed solution is regulation. If frontier AI eventually requires enormously expensive safety testing, auditing, cybersecurity and government compliance, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google can pay for it. Two blokes with a promising model and a WeWork membership probably cannot.A safety barrier can also become a moat.So, there is a network, remarkable timing and legitimate questions, but not proof of a conspiracy.Rosa Parks was not an accidental symbol either: her refusal to surrender her seat was not staged, but civil-rights organisers had been looking for a strong test case against bus segregation and deliberately rallied around Parks after earlier cases, including Claudette Colvin. The strategic choice of messenger did not make segregation any less real.Gary Marcus, one of OpenAI’s greatest critics, makes the most logical yet sceptical argument. He thinks the existential threat is “greatly exaggerated”, but his point about Coxon was simpler: forget the biography and ask whether the man is actually right.And just when the whole thing starts looking too perfectly packaged, reality inconveniently gives the doomers something to work with. Anthropic released a threat report describing attempts to use Claude for cyber operations, weapons work and potentially dangerous biological research, including gain-of-function work involving chikungunya. The cases predated Coxon’s resignation, but the timing was almost offensively perfect, rather like Nvidia agreeing to acquire Hugging Face for $12.93 billion days after OpenAI publicly disclosed the July incident.Anthropic also revealed that a weapons-development cell in northern Yemen had used Claude Code to help develop guidance, navigation and control software for a guided rocket, a long-range ballistic missile and a hypersonic-glide variant. The cell even test-fired the guided rocket, apparently failed, and returned to Claude to figure out what had gone wrong.Perhaps the question here isn’t existential but what the Romans called, or who benefits, because incentives matter. Someone can profit from pointing out that your house is on fire, even while the fact remains that perhaps your house is on fire.American author Upton Sinclair famously observed that it is difficult to make a man understand something when his salary depends upon his not understanding it. AI has produced the funhouse-mirror version: what happens when your salary, your company valuation and your sincere belief that you are saving humanity all depend upon understanding the world in exactly the same way?The optimists say AI will cure diseases, create abundance and even solve Navier-Stokes, though how that improves our lives is beyond me.The doomers say the same technology might destroy civilisation.Opposite advertisements, same product: AI is the most important thing in the world. One tells investors they cannot afford to miss it; the other tells governments they cannot afford to ignore it. And the jokers point out that the idea of being killed by a Chinese robot is ridiculous. The world-ending — as all Hollywood movies have predicted — should be conceived in America.The behaviour of AI companies, from OpenAI, which started as a non-profit, to whatever it is today, to Anthropic, which built itself around AI safety while also being the guy building the killer robot because how else will we know how to defend ourselves, hardly makes the answer easier.Anthropic has reached a similar bind. It built itself around AI safety but believes meaningful safety research requires remaining near the frontier.Max Weber, the German sociologist who studied capitalism and bureaucracy, used the idea of the “iron cage” to describe how rational institutions can eventually trap the people inside them. Everyone might be following perfectly logical rules from his own position, but the system itself begins deciding what behaviour is rational, making it increasingly difficult for anyone inside it to simply stop and we appear to be in the iron cage now.Nobody inside it needs to be lying because the system supplies the justification.Perhaps Big Tech is hyping doomsday because fear brings money, attention and regulation.Perhaps they believe humanity is playing Russian roulette.Or perhaps all of them are partly right or wrong.Human beings have always been good at discovering that whatever advances our interests also happens to be morally necessary. As the saying goes, once you have got them by the profit sheets, the hearts and minds will follow.The irony of AI alignment may be that we spent years worrying about machines rationalising their objectives while the species building them has been practising that trick since we came down from the trees.Hopefully, whatever version of doomsday the AI world is worried about waits until after, because after all the multiverse nonsense and speculation about how Robert Downey Jr is going to return to the MCU as Doctor Doom, one really wants to watch Kevin Feige explain that before artificial intelligence kills everyone.And after that, if one has to be killed by a robot, let it be an American one (with an Austrian accent), not a Chinese one. What could be more ridiculous than that?
Article Summary: Marvel Studios is as good a metaphor for what happens when a company starts believing in its own infallibility. The jury — Reddit fanboys of Marvel — are trying to figure out how the geniuses at Marvel will tie it all in. Some of the people closest to building the world’s most powerful AI systems are openly saying that those systems might kill all of us.

Article Title: Elon Musk's Cybercab has no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors; US safety regulators open audit of about 1,000 cars over Tesla's self-certification
Article Text:
"Tesla historically has tested limits and pushed boundaries on regulations,"

"I fully expect Tesla to test the limits."

"creative interpretation"

"flood the market"

"That could take NHTSA or state regulators years to resolve. Meanwhile, Tesla could be operating on public roads."

A vehicle without conventional controls

"No public information about Tesla's capabilities suggests that Tesla is anywhere close to being able to safely and reliably deploy an automated driving system over the wide range of conditions that would be required for a vehicle without conventional controls,"

A path to public roads

"It does happen from time to time and NHTSA, importantly, has not always won these cases,"

Tesla's race to deploy its Cybercab robotaxis is testing US vehicle-safety rules. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, this comes as the Elon Musk-led electric-car maker begins offering paid rides in two-seat vehicles that operate without a steering wheel, pedals or conventional mirrors.Just hours after an event in downtown Austin, Texas, marking the rollout, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said it had opened an audit of about 1,000 Cybercab vehicles, the Reuters report noted. The review will examine how Tesla determined that the cars comply with federal vehicle-safety regulations.US regulations on the commercialisation of vehicles that fail to meet federal safety standards were mostly created with human-driven cars in mind and require manual operation. However, these regulations have loopholes, and Tesla CEO Elon Musk is well aware of them.Amid a crowd of Tesla fans and social media influencers in downtown Austin, Tesla added Cybercabs to its robotaxi fleet, which already operates the company's best-selling Model Y SUVs. Tesla said Cybercab rides would be open to everyone, and executives discussed pricing plans.The golden-coloured Cybercab, fitted with butterfly doors, is central to Musk's strategy of relying on self-driving software and robotics.That strategy has helped push Tesla's stock valuation to about $1.4 trillion, exceeding the combined value of several of the world's largest automakers.Unlike many other countries, the US does not generally require automakers to obtain regulatory clearance for a new vehicle model and its technology before putting it on public roads. Instead, manufacturers can deploy vehicles by self-certifying that they meet federal safety standards."I don't think there is a reasonable interpretation that can be made to suggest that the Cybercab can comply with the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards," Michael Brooks, executive director of the Center for Auto Safety, a consumer advocacy group told Reuters.At the same time, NHTSA is moving to change vehicle-safety standards and is separately drafting rules intended to accommodate driverless vehicles. Industry experts have said those changes are likely to take longer to take effect than the timeline Elon Musk has promised for the Cybercab.Elon Musk has previously shown a willingness to challenge regulations.said Philip Koopman, a Carnegie Mellon University engineering professor and autonomous-vehicle safety expert.Koopman said Musk could come up with aof vehicle regulation, say that Cybercabs comply with federal standards andwith them.The Cybercab manufacturing process began in April, and Musk has promised that the production rate will increase exponentially either late this year or early next year. In addition, Musk said the Cybercab would cost less than $30,000 when it was introduced in 2024.Furthermore, Tesla has started providing its customers with a robotaxi service in Texas and Florida; however, this service is only available with the Model Y SUV. The vehicles are autonomous; however, they still have manual controls, which certain regulations and manufacturers mandate.The Cybercab's uniqueness lies in its lack of controls found in conventional vehicles. Specialists have raised concerns about the autonomous driving capabilities of vehicles manufactured by Tesla.Tesla has said its Full Self-Driving software, which powers the Cybercab, is up to 10 times safer than human drivers. The company's Austin robotaxi service has also operated without a fatal accident. However, Reuters interviews with several former Tesla employees who trained the company's self-driving software found that it continued to struggle with basic driving manoeuvres.said Bryant Walker Smith, a University of South Carolina law professor focused on autonomous-driving regulation.The issue concerns federal safety standards for automobiles drafted for manually operated cars. The issue arises because cars with automated driving systems lack some controls needed to comply with the standards.For vehicles that do not comply with federal safety standards, NHTSA has an exemption process that allows automakers to seek permission for limited deployment. That route, however, currently caps deployment at 2,500 vehicles a year.Tesla's engineering chief Lars Moravy said on social media platform X earlier this year that the Cybercab would not be subject to that cap, although he did not explain why. NHTSA has previously said Tesla had not applied for an exemption.That has led to speculation that Tesla may have instead chosen to self-certify the Cybercab, as Koopman suggested.A precedent already exists involving another autonomous vehicle without conventional driving controls. Amazon's Zoox, which is developing a vehicle with two bench seats facing each other and no driving controls, also attempted to use the self-certification route.Zoox declared its car safe to operate, but it retracted that statement when NHTSA decided to investigate. About a year later, in July, Zoox received a government exemption.Any dispute between NHTSA and Tesla over the Cybercab's self-certification could eventually end up in court, according to three former senior NHTSA officials who spoke to Reuters before Thursday's event.one of the former officials said.
Article Summary: Tesla's race to deploy its Cybercab robotaxis is testing US vehicle-safety rules. This comes as the Elon Musk-led electric-car maker begins offering paid rides in two-seat vehicles that operate without a steering wheel, pedals or conventional mirrors. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said it had opened an audit of about 1,000 Cybercabs.
